EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted portions of far southeastern Kansas from January 23���25, 2026, bringing significant snow, ice, record-breaking cold to the region. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas. Limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to remain across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across portions of far southeastern Kansas. Through the month, the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southeastern Kansas shrank significantly. By the end of the month only small areas Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained across southern portions of Cherokee County. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around 8 PM on 13 April 2026, an EF-1 tornado associated with|a supercell developed in far southwest Linn County, KS, around|2 miles southeast of the town of Blue Mound near the intersection|of 300th Road and Farris Rd. The tornado tracked to the east|northeast, causing significant tree damage to a home off Ingrahm|Road. From there, the tornado crossed Kansas Highway 31/52 and|caused significant damage to trees at Curry Cemetery and then|caused damage to trees and outbuildings along 600th Road. The tornado|continued into the Sugar Valley and Hidden Valley Lakes community,|flipping over campers, damaging trees and docks, and throwing|a manufactured home off its cinder block supports, completely|destroying it, near Park Lane and Paine Road, where 2 people|sustained injuries. Continuing further to the east northeast,|the tornado caused significant tree and outbuilding damage to|a residence along Scott Road north of 750th Road, and then crossed|US Highway 69 about 2 miles south of Pleasanton and continued|all the way to the Missouri State Line just north of 1100th Road,|primarily damaging trees. The tornado continued into Bates County,|Missouri, damaging trees in the community of Worland, ending|shortly east northeast of Worland around 8:46 PM CDT. In total,|the tornado traveled around 24 miles over the course of 43 minutes,|with a peak wind of 105 mph.

Initial damage was confined to the campground and park|headquarters. The tornado strengthened to an EF-1 as it followed W|255th St and crossed Harmony Rd. The Tornado continued east|toward the town of Hillsdale, KS. The tornado began to weaken as it crossed rural areas,|before ending just short of US Hwy 169 north of 255th St.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey revealed a tornado formed a few miles west of Ottawa and proceeded to move ESE through the southern parts of the city of Ottawa.  The tornado turned to the ENE as it exited to the city and moved across interstate 35 doing more damage to structures before it ended near the Marais des Cygness River. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms developed along and ahead of a cold front late in the afternoon on Friday April 17th.  Storms organized into a short line that begin to prouce damaging downdraft winds.  A small tornado also formed on the northern side of the short line and produced damage in the town of Olivet in Osage County.  A damage survey was done the next day and it was found to be EF1 damage mainly to outbuildings along with tree limb damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS tornado damage survey revealed a short path small tornado produced damage in the town of Olivet.  A few outbuidings were damaged or destroyed and several large trees were uprooted or had broken branches.  The damage was determined to be EF1 with winds to around 100-105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Moderate (D1) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas but limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to develop across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought expanding leaving Severe (D2) drought, Moderate (D1) drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.
